en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Chapter on the Power of Supernatural Faculties from the Section of Puzzling Questions (Meṇḍakapañha)
5. The Question of King Sivi’s Gift of Eyes:
“Venerable Nāgasena, you say this:
‘King Sivi gave his eyes to a beggar, and although he was blind, divine eyes arose in him once again.’”

This statement is also deceitful, refutable, and faulty, for it contradicts the Sutta which says: "When the cause has been eradicated, being without cause and without basis, there is no arising of the divine eye.
If, venerable Nāgasena, King Sivi gave his eyes to the beggar, then that statement that "the divine eyes arose again" must be false.
“If divine eyes have arisen [in you], then the statement that ‘King Sivi gave his eyes to the beggar’ is also false.

This question, which has two sides, is more knotty than a knot, more entangled than an entanglement, and more impenetrable than a thicket; it has come before you. Therefore, rouse your zeal for its resolution, for the refutation of opposing views, and for their subjugation.”
“Great King, the eyes were given by King Sivi to the beggar; do not entertain doubt regarding that. Furthermore, divine eyes arose [in him]; do not entertain doubt regarding that either.
“But, venerable Nāgasena, when the cause has been eradicated, does the divine eye arise in one who is without cause and without basis?
“No, Great King,” [he replied].

“But what, venerable sir, is the reason here, by which reason, when the cause has been uprooted, being without cause and without basis, the divine eye arises? Pray, convince me by means of that reason.
“But what, great king, is there in the world called ‘truth,’ by which those who speak the truth perform an act of truth?
“Yes, venerable sir, there is in the world what is called truth; for by truth, venerable Nāgasena, those who speak the truth perform an act of truth.”
“Having performed this, they cause the gods to rain, they extinguish fires, they counteract poison, and they perform various other deeds that ought to be done.
“In that case, Great King, it is logical and consistent that divine vision arose for King Sivi through the power of truth.
For, Great King, by the power of truth, divine vision arises even where there is no physical basis; truth itself is the basis in that case.”
It conduces to the arising of the divine eye.
Just as, O Great King, whatever beings chant a truth saying, “May a great rain-cloud pour forth,” for them the great rain-cloud pours forth simultaneously with that chanting of the truth;
yet, O Great King, is there any cause for rain in the sky?
“Is there a cause by which a great cloud pours down rain?”—“No indeed, venerable sir;
truth itself is the cause for the pouring down of a great cloud.”—“In the same way, Great King, that divine eye has no natural cause; truth alone is the basis here for the arising of the divine eye.”
Or again, Great King, suppose there are certain beings who utter a truth, saying, ‘May this great mass of blazing, fiercely burning fire turn back!
With the utterance of that truth, the great mass of blazing, fiercely burning fire turns back in an instant.
Now, Great King, is there any accumulated cause within that great mass of blazing, fiercely burning fire by which reason the great mass of blazing, fiercely burning fire turns back in an instant?”
“Certainly not, venerable sir; truth alone is the basis for the immediate turning back of that great mass of blazing, fiercely burning fire.
“In the same way, Great King, there is no other natural cause; truth alone is the basis here for the arising of the divine eye.
Or again, Great King, it is like those beings who recite the truth: ‘Let the deadly *halāhala* poison become an antidote (*agada*).’”

“Simultaneously with the chanting of the Truth, their Halāhala poison becomes an antidote in an instant. Now, Great King, is there any accumulated cause within that Halāhala poison by which the Halāhala poison becomes an antidote in an instant?
“No indeed, Bhante; the Truth itself is the cause therein for the instantaneous neutralization of the Halāhala poison.”
“In the same way, Great King, even without a natural cause, truth alone serves as the basis here for the arising of the divine eye.
For the penetration of the four noble truths, Great King, there is no other basis; making truth the basis, one penetrates the four noble truths.
Great King, there was a king of China in the land of China who, desiring to sport in the great ocean, [would go] every four months.”
Having performed an act of truth, he enters a league into the great ocean together with his chariot;
before the front of his chariot, a great mass of water recedes, and as he emerges, it flows back over him.
Now, Great King, would that great ocean be capable of being made to recede by the natural bodily strength of the world, including its gods and humans?”

“Venerable sir, even in a very small pond, it would not be possible for the world—including its gods and humans—to turn back the water by means of ordinary physical strength; how much more so, then, the water in the great ocean?
“For this reason too, Great King, the power of truth should be known: ‘There is no place that cannot be reached by truth.
Great King, in the city of Pāṭaliputta, King Aśoka the Dhamma-king [was accompanied] by his townspeople, countryfolk, ministers, soldiers, and high officials...”
Seeing the river Gaṅgā, filled with fresh water, level with its banks, brimming, five hundred yojanas in length,
one yojana in width, and flowing on, he surrounded by his ministers spoke thus:
“Is there anyone, I say, who is capable of making this great Gaṅgā flow upstream?”
The ministers said, “It is difficult, Your Majesty.
Standing on that very bank of the Ganges, a courtesan named Bandhumatī heard what the king had said:
“Is it possible to make this great Ganges flow upstream? She spoke thus:
“I am indeed a courtesan living by my beauty, a woman of the lowest livelihood in the city of Pāṭaliputta; let the King witness my declaration of truth.

Then she made her declaration of truth, and simultaneously with that declaration of truth, while the great multitude of people looked on, the Mahāgaṅgā began to flow back upstream with a gurgling roar.

Then the King, hearing the terrifying sound produced by the whirlpools and the force of the waves in the Gaṅgā, was struck with wonder, filled with amazement and astonishment, and spoke thus to his ministers:
“Tell me, my man, why is this great Ganges River flowing upstream?
“Great King, having heard your words, the courtesan Bandhumatī performed an act of truth; by that act of truth, the great Ganges is flowing upstream.
Then, with a heart filled with agitation, the king went in great haste and questioned the courtesan himself.
“Is it true, sir, that by means of this act of truth you caused this Ganges to flow upstream?
“Yes, Your Majesty,” he replied.
The king said:
"What power do you have there, or who would heed your words while sane? By what power did you cause this great Ganges to flow upstream?
She replied, "By the power of truth, Great King, I caused this great Ganges to flow upstream."
The king said:
"What power of truth do you possess—you who are a thief, a harlot, lacking mindfulness, a cutpurse, a wicked woman, one of broken virtue, one who has transcended shame, and a seducer of blind folk?
"Truth, Great King, I do have; such as I am, O Great King, even for one like me there exists an act of truth by which, if I so desired, I could overturn the world together with its devas."
The king said:
“But what is this ‘act of truth’? Pray, tell it to me.
“Great King, whoever gives me wealth—whether a kshatriya, a brahmin, a vaisya, a sudra, or anyone else—”
“I attend upon them all equally; there is no distinction such as ‘he is a khattiya,’ nor is there any contempt such as ‘he is a suddo.
Free from both attraction and aversion, I serve the master of my wealth. This, O King, is my act of truth (saccakiriyā), by which I have caused this great Ganges to flow upstream.”
Thus, Great King, those established in truth do not fail to find any benefit whatsoever.
And, Great King, the eyes given by King Sivi to the beggar became divine eyes (*dibbacakkhu*), and that was through the power of his declaration of truth (*saccakiriyā*).
As for what is stated in the Sutta:
“When the fleshly eye has perished—being without cause and without basis—there is no arising of the divine eye.
This was said with reference to the eye consisting of mental development; thus you should bear this in mind, O Great King.
“Excellent, Bhante Nāgasena! The question has been well unraveled, the refutation well demonstrated, and the opposing views well crushed. Thus it is; so do I accept it.”
The fifth question: The Gift of Eyes by King Sivi.
